power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: We find that a vast space of public health interventions necessarily reshape the intervals between successive infections, known as generation times, for directly-transmitted infectious diseases (e.g.,  Ebola virus, influenza).
While some studies have connected specific interventions (e.g., contact-tracing, isolation) to shifted generation times, most epidemiological analyses assume these intervals are stationary.
We reveal that this assumption is substantially more fragile than previously recognised.

We develop a universal microscopic representation for all intervention mechanisms that reduce individual-level infectiousness and establish generation-time reshaping as a fundamental macroscopic feature of those interventions, emerging at the population level.
By constraining the topology of our representation to reflect specific mechanisms, we explain and unify previous studies as well as predict generation-time phenomena yet to be observed.
We further show that neglecting generation-time reshaping can under-or over-estimate intervention effectiveness and disease controllability by 100%, under realistic parameter settings.
A stringent intervention can even produce no estimated transmissibility difference.
Generation-time distortion causes unavoidable and underrated biases that can severely limit model-driven public health policy and pandemic preparedness.
Introduction.
Measuring the effectiveness of epidemic interventions is of fundamental public health importance.

Prospective estimates of how available control actions limit transmission are critical for pandemic preparedness and have informed vaccination, lockdown and travel policies as well as biothreat risk assessments [1] [2] [3] [4].

We formulate a universal but minimal microscopic intervention mechanism to test our effect models.
Consider a newly infected individual so their age since infection is s = 0.

On applying an intervention this individual is recurrently subject, as s ticks, to an arbitrary combination of detection and control stages (e.g., testing, antivirals, isolation) that suppress their ability to mix and transmit.
While under control, the individual faces opportunities to exit (e.g., non-compliance, early release).
We can represent every such mechanism with an ageinhomogeneous hidden Markov model (HMM), in which the individual progresses through arbitrary mixing M (blue) and non-mixing M c (red) states.
We illustrate key mappings between primitive HMM motifs and interventions in Table I.
text.formatted: We illustrate key mappings between primitive HMM motifs and interventions in Table <ref type="table">I</ref>.

text.text: Our representation covers all interventions that act by reducing infectiousness after infection.
Motifs with non-mixing absorbing states model controls such as isolation and quarantine.
Those with mixing absorbing states model release and non-compliance.
We can extend both motifs using phase-type pipelines, which realise any positive-valued distribution by flexibly wiring internal states in series and parallel.

These can model arbitrary delays to detection, treatment or release, 120 presymptomatic spread, population heterogeneity, multi-121 ple transmission routes, risk-sensitive behaviour and tar-122 geted action, among others.
By combining our primitive 123 topologies, we can approximate arbitrarily complex inter-124 vention mechanisms.

However, this description does not 125 model interventions acting primarily through susceptibil-126 ity reduction, such as shielding or vaccines and tracing 127 that prevent infection instead of transmission.
